perspective:
**Harold Padilla’s available information:**

- He is a project manager dealing with a project team whose progress is frustrating him.
- He felt frustrated and anxious, believing his team was not performing well because they lacked motivation.
- He knows Arthur Begum as a friend/police officer he turns to for advice, and he arranged a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur.
- In that meeting, Harold told Arthur his team seemed completely unmotivated and that it was affecting progress. Arthur suggested understanding what drives each team member individually and having one-on-one conversations.
- Harold decided to try Arthur’s advice and felt more hopeful.
- Harold then told his team he wanted one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them. Team Member 1 said it could be helpful. Team Member 2 said they were open to it. Harold said he would schedule time with each of them.
- After implementing this, Harold noticed the team still was not responding well. He felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future.
- Harold told Arthur the suggestions had not worked. Arthur suggested there might be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors. Harold decided to investigate further.
- Harold held one-on-one meetings. Team Member 1 told him there was tension among a few team members affecting work. Harold said he would look into resolving the conflicts.
- Team Member 2 told Harold they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed, making it hard to stay motivated. Harold said he would see about redistributing tasks and that their well-being was important.
- Harold then felt optimistic and empowered, believing that addressing individual concerns would improve team performance.
- He told the team he would implement regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. Team Member 1 said that sounded great. Team Member 2 agreed it was good their concerns were being addressed.
- Harold said he was glad and that their input and well-being were crucial to the project’s success.

Harold does **not** have access to the private thoughts, hidden motivations, personality labels, or unspoken information of Arthur or the team members beyond what they directly said or what he observed.
